Observability for Event-Driven Architectures

Example Weekly — engineering practice column. Saved offline snapshot.

Event-driven systems fail in the gaps between services, so the unit of observability is the event's journey, not any single process. Teams that instrument only service-local metrics discover incidents through customer reports; teams that trace the event corridor see the same incidents as a latency spike on one hop.

Three practices separate mature setups from the rest. First, propagate a correlation identifier end to end — producer, broker, consumer — so any message can be followed across hops. Second, budget cardinality deliberately: per-tenant labels are useful, per-message labels are a metrics-backend outage waiting to happen. Third, alert on consumer lag trends rather than absolute thresholds; a queue that drains in five minutes every morning is normal, and the same queue draining in fifty is an incident even when the absolute depth looks small.

The column's recurring conclusion: the broker is part of the observable system. Broker-side metrics (partition skew, redelivery counts, dead-letter depth) belong on the same dashboards as service metrics, or the corridor view stays blind in exactly the place failures concentrate.
